node.title: Mitochondrial number and cell energy demand
node.canonical_question: Why do heart muscle cells have far more mitochondria than skin cells?
node.summary: Heart muscle contracts continuously and needs a vast and steady supply of ATP. Cells match mitochondrial number to their energy demand, so high-demand cells contain many more mitochondria. Skin cells are largely quiescent and require far less ATP.

core.explanation:
The number of mitochondria in a cell reflects that cell's energy demand. Because mitochondria are the main site of ATP production through oxidative phosphorylation, a cell that constantly needs large amounts of ATP must house many of them.

Heart muscle (cardiac muscle) contracts rhythmically every second of your life without rest. Each contraction requires ATP to power the myosin motors that pull actin filaments together. The heart cannot pause to recover, so it depends on a continuous, high-rate supply of ATP. To meet this demand, roughly 25 to 35 percent of the volume of a cardiac muscle cell is occupied by mitochondria.

Skin cells (particularly keratinocytes in the outer epidermis) have a very different role. They form a protective barrier, a task that requires relatively little ongoing ATP compared with sustained mechanical work. Their metabolic rate is low, so they maintain far fewer mitochondria.

This relationship between energy demand and mitochondrial number is a general principle. Neurons, liver cells, and skeletal muscle fibres in endurance athletes are other examples of cell types that are rich in mitochondria precisely because their functions are energetically expensive. Conversely, red blood cells contain no mitochondria at all and rely entirely on glycolysis.

Cells can also adjust their mitochondrial number over time. Endurance exercise training signals cardiac and skeletal muscle cells to grow more mitochondria (mitochondrial biogenesis), increasing their capacity for aerobic ATP production.
key_points: Cells match the number of mitochondria to their rate of ATP consumption.
Cardiac muscle contracts without rest and needs a continuous high ATP supply, so 25 to 35 percent of its volume is mitochondria.
Skin cells form a passive barrier and have a low metabolic rate, requiring far fewer mitochondria.
Other high-demand cell types such as neurons and liver cells are also mitochondria-rich.
Mitochondrial number is not fixed: exercise and other signals can trigger mitochondrial biogenesis.

rendering.summary: Heart muscle never stops beating and burns huge amounts of ATP every second, so it is packed with mitochondria. Skin cells sit in a protective layer and do relatively little work, so they only need a small number. Cells simply build as many mitochondria as their energy needs require.
rendering.analogy: Think of mitochondria as generators in a building. A hospital running round the clock needs rows of backup generators. A garden shed needs at most one. The number of generators matches the power demand of the building.
